title: Static electricity — why you get zapped touching a door handle
examTip: Static electricity questions almost always ask about electron transfer. Never say protons move. Say which object gains or loses electrons, and what charge each ends up with.
introTips: Think of a time you got a static shock. That tiny spark is the same physics as a lightning bolt, just on a very different scale.
Before reading, try this. In one sentence, explain why your hair can stand on end after you rub a balloon on it.
Focus on which way the electrons move. Which object gains them, which loses them, and what charge results?
intro: You walk across a carpet, touch a door handle and get a small shock. That is caused by the same basic physics as a lightning strike. In both cases, charge builds up and then jumps through the air as a spark. Static electricity explains everyday shocks, clinging clothes and lightning.

keyPoints.heading: Charging by rubbing
keyPoints.content: When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons are transferred from one surface to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses electrons becomes positively charged. Key rule: only electrons transfer. Protons are fixed inside atomic nuclei and cannot be moved by rubbing. Charge is conserved: one material gains a negative charge, and the other is left with an equal positive charge. Examples: - a polythene rod rubbed with a cloth gains electrons from the cloth. The polythene becomes negative, and the cloth becomes positive - an acetate rod rubbed with a cloth loses electrons to the cloth. The acetate becomes positive, and the cloth becomes negative Certain insulators become charged when rubbed against each other. A metal door handle is a conductor. Charge flows through it easily. This is why it discharges you at once. The charge flows through the conductor. But a polythene rod stays charged.
writeBullets: Rubbing transfers electrons, never protons. Protons are fixed in the nucleus
Object gaining electrons → negatively charged
Object losing electrons → positively charged
Charge is conserved: one material gains a negative charge, and the other is left with an equal positive charge
Polythene + cloth: polythene gains electrons → negative. Cloth → positive
Acetate + cloth: acetate loses electrons → positive. Cloth → negative

keyTerms.def: The transfer of electrons between two insulating surfaces when rubbed together, causing one to become positive and the other negative.
The material that loses electrons is left with a positive charge. It is equal in size to the negative charge on the other material.
A material that does not allow charge to flow through it easily; static charge can build up on insulators.

keyPoints.memTip: Electrons are the movers. Think of them as passengers getting off one bus and onto another. The bus that loses passengers (electrons) goes positive. The one that gains them goes negative.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The single most common mistake in static electricity questions is writing 'protons are transferred'. It must be electrons. Repeat this rule until it is automatic.

keyPoints.heading: Same and different types of charge
keyPoints.content: Two objects that carry different types of charge attract. Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel. You can show this simply. Hang two negatively charged polythene rods near each other on threads. They swing apart (repel). Bring a negatively charged rod near a positively charged acetate rod. They swing towards each other (attract). The force between charges gets weaker as the distance between them grows. Everyday examples of static attraction and repulsion: - clothes clinging after a tumble dryer: electrons move from one fabric to another. One gains electrons and one loses them, so they attract - hair standing on end after pulling off a jumper: electrons move between the jumper and your hair. The strands all get the same charge, so they repel Lightning: when enough charge builds up in a storm cloud, a huge spark jumps between the cloud and the ground. That is a lightning bolt.
writeBullets: Same type of charge: repel. Different types of charge: attract
The force between charges gets weaker as the distance grows
Two rods with the same type of charge: repel (swing apart on threads)
Two rods with different types of charge: attract (swing together)
Lightning: a huge spark between a charged storm cloud and the ground
Hair standing on end: electrons are transferred, so the strands all have the same charge → they repel each other

keyTerms.def: The force pulling objects together; two objects that carry different types of charge attract.
The force pushing objects apart; two objects that carry the same type of charge repel.
A huge spark from a charged storm cloud, to another cloud or to the ground.

keyPoints.memTip: Same type of charge: they push each other away (repel). Different types of charge: they pull together (attract).
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say 'positive attracts positive'. The same type of charge repels. Different types of charge attract. Getting this backwards costs marks on every static question.

keyPoints.heading: Electric fields
keyPoints.content: A charged object creates an electric field in the space around it. Any other charged object placed in this field feels a force. This is a non-contact force: the objects do not need to touch. An electric field is shown by field lines. These show the direction of the force on a small positive test charge. - Around an isolated charged sphere, the field lines are straight. They meet the surface at right angles. - For a positive sphere, the field lines point outward. A positive test charge would be pushed away. - For a negative sphere, the field lines point inward. A positive test charge would be pulled in. A stronger electric field is shown by closer (more dense) field lines. The field gets weaker with distance from a charged object, like a gravitational field.
writeBullets: Charged objects create an electric field in the space around them. No contact is needed
Non-contact force — charged objects exert forces on each other without touching
Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive test charge
Isolated charged sphere: straight field lines at right angles to the surface
Positive sphere: field lines point outward. Negative sphere: field lines point inward
Closer field lines → stronger electric field

keyTerms.def: A region of space around a charged object where another charge experiences a force.
Lines drawn to represent an electric field; show the direction of force on a positive test charge. Closer lines = stronger field.

keyPoints.memTip: Field lines are like arrows showing where a positive charge would go. From a positive source, the arrows flee outward.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Draw field lines around an isolated charged sphere as straight lines at right angles to the surface. Add arrows: outward for positive, inward for negative.

keyPoints.heading: Sparking
keyPoints.content: Sparking happens when charge jumps through the air. A highly charged object has a strong electric field around it. If the field is strong enough, electrons can jump through the air to or from a nearby object. This is a spark. You see this when you touch a door handle after walking on a carpet. Rubbing your feet on the carpet transfers electrons, so you become charged. Electrons then jump between your hand and the handle. Lightning is the same thing on a huge scale. Dangers: static sparks carry enough energy to ignite flammable vapours. Even a small spark near fuel vapour can cause an explosion.
writeBullets: Sparking — electrons jump through the air between objects
A strong electric field near a highly charged object makes charge jump
Static spark danger: sparks can ignite flammable vapours

keyTerms.def: Charge jumping through the air when the electric field near a charged object is strong enough.

keyPoints.tutor_note: When you explain a spark, mention the electric field. A strong field near a charged object makes charge jump through the air.

tables.title: Charging by rubbing — summary
rows: Electrons transfer FROM cloth TO polythene
Electrons transfer FROM acetate TO cloth
Electrons transfer from hair to balloon
Positive (why hair stands up — strands repel)

0.question: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. What has happened to make the rod negatively charged?
options: Electrons have transferred from the cloth to the polythene rod
Protons have transferred from the polythene to the cloth
Electrons have transferred from the polythene to the cloth
The cloth has given the rod extra neutrons
0.correctFeedback: Exactly right. Electrons move from the cloth onto the polythene. The rod gains electrons and becomes negative. The cloth loses electrons and becomes positive.
0.wrongFeedback: Only electrons transfer. Protons and neutrons cannot be moved by rubbing. The polythene becomes negative because it GAINS electrons from the cloth, not because it loses anything.

1.question: Two polythene rods are both negatively charged and hung near each other. What will happen?
options: They will repel each other (move apart)
They will attract each other (move together)
One will become positive and attract the other
1.correctFeedback: Correct. The same type of charge repels. Both rods are negative, so they push each other away.
1.wrongFeedback: Remember: the same type of charge REPELS. Both rods are negative, so they push each other away. Attraction only happens between different types of charge.

2.question: Which describes the electric field lines around an isolated positively charged sphere?
options: Straight lines at right angles to the surface, pointing outward
Straight lines at right angles to the surface, pointing inward
Lines that only appear when another charge touches the sphere
2.correctFeedback: Correct. The field lines are straight and meet the surface at right angles. For a positive sphere they point outward.
2.wrongFeedback: Field lines show the force on a positive test charge. A positive sphere pushes it away, so the lines point outward. They are straight and at right angles to the surface.

3.question: Why can a spark jump from a highly charged object to a nearby object?
options: The electric field near the object is strong enough to make charge jump through the air
The force between charges gets stronger with distance
The nearby object must be an insulator
3.correctFeedback: Correct. A highly charged object has a strong electric field. If it is strong enough, charge jumps through the air as a spark.
3.wrongFeedback: Sparking is explained by the electric field. Near a highly charged object the field is strong. If it is strong enough, charge jumps through the air.

commonMistakes: Writing that protons transfer during charging by rubbing. Only electrons can move. Protons are locked inside the atomic nucleus and cannot be moved by rubbing.
Saying the same type of charge attracts. This is the opposite of the rule. The same type of charge REPELS. Different types of charge ATTRACT.
Drawing electric field lines around a negative charge pointing outward. Field lines always point inward towards a negative charge. That is the way a positive test charge would move.
Mixing up 'charged' with 'has more protons'. Charge comes from gaining or losing electrons. It does not come from changing the number of protons.
examTips: When asked to explain charging by rubbing, always say three things. (1) What transfers: electrons. (2) Which way they move: from ___ to ___. (3) What charge each object ends up with. Three steps, three marks.
For electric field questions, remember: field lines show the direction of the force on a POSITIVE test charge. Around positive = outward. Around negative = inward.
revisionCardBullets: Rubbing transfers electrons only, never protons
Object gains electrons → negatively charged. Loses electrons → positively charged
Charge is conserved: one material gains a negative charge, and the other is left with an equal positive charge
Same type of charge repels. Different types of charge attract
The force between charges gets weaker with distance
Electric field: region where a charge experiences a force
Field lines: the direction of the force on a positive test charge. Positive source → outward. Negative source → inward
Isolated charged sphere: straight field lines at right angles to the surface
Sparking: a strong electric field makes charge jump through the air
